title: “DRINK WATER FROM YOUR OWN CISTERN”: WAS PROVERBS REALLY TALKING ABOUT SEXUAL FAITHFULNESS?
paragraphs: “DRINK WATER FROM YOUR OWN CISTERN”: WAS PROVERBS REALLY TALKING ABOUT SEXUAL FAITHFULNESS?

Proverbs 5:15 sounds almost innocent—until you discover what the “water,” the “cistern,” and the “fountain” are doing in the rest of the chapter. Then one ancient sentence becomes an alarmingly intimate message about desire, marriage, temptation, adultery…and the God who refuses to let lust have the final word.
There are Bible verses we read quickly because we think we already understand them.
Then there are verses that stop looking innocent when you read what comes before and after them.
Proverbs 5:15 is one of those verses.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Beautiful.
Poetic.
Almost peaceful.
But Solomon was not giving his son advice about staying hydrated.
He was talking about sex.
More specifically, he was teaching something our generation desperately needs to hear:
Your desires are powerful, but they were never meant to become your master.
And if you keep reading, Proverbs does something surprising.
It does not merely tell a married man, “Don’t commit adultery.”
It tells him where his desire belongs.
The original Hebrew reads:
שְׁתֵה־מַיִם מִבּוֹרֶךָ וְנֹזְלִים מִתּוֹךְ בְּאֵרֶךָ
Sheteh-mayim miborekha, wenozelim mittokh be’erekha.
Literally, the imagery is straightforward:
“Drink water from your own cistern, and flowing water from your own well.”
The Hebrew verb שְׁתֵה — sheteh means “drink.”
מַיִם — mayim means “water.”
בּוֹר — bor refers to a pit or cistern, a place where water was gathered and preserved.
And בְּאֵר — be’er means a well.
But here is where everything changes.
You cannot correctly interpret verse 15 by ripping it away from Proverbs 5.
Because this entire chapter is a father warning his son about sexual temptation.
Earlier, he warns about the “strange woman” or forbidden woman.
Her lips drip sweetness.
Her speech is seductive.
Everything about temptation initially promises pleasure.
Then Scripture pulls back the curtain.
What tastes like honey eventually becomes bitter.
What looks like freedom can become slavery.
What promises excitement can leave destruction behind.
And suddenly that ancient warning does not feel ancient anymore.
Because maybe your temptation does not stand on a street corner.
Maybe it lives behind a screen.
Maybe it arrives through a private message.
Maybe it has a profile picture.
Maybe it begins with a conversation you know you should end.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows you watch.
Maybe it is the coworker whose attention feels dangerously good.
Maybe it is the former relationship you keep checking.
Maybe it is the emotional affair you keep calling “friendship.”
Maybe nothing physical has happened.
Yet.
But somewhere inside, you already know why you keep returning.
And Scripture whispers across thousands of years:
Drink from your own cistern.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God understands its power.
That distinction matters.
Christian teaching about sexuality is sometimes reduced to a giant list of prohibitions.
Don’t do this.
Don’t look there.
Don’t touch that.
Don’t desire this.
But Proverbs 5 does something far richer.
It warns against forbidden sexuality, yes.
Then it turns toward marital delight.
A few verses later we read:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorekha barukh, usemach me’eshet ne’urekha.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth.”
There it is.
The metaphor opens.
The cistern.
The well.
The fountain.
The wife.
The covenant.
The rejoicing.
This is not a picture of sexuality as dirty.
It is a picture of sexuality as powerful enough to require covenant.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
He created the human body.
He created attraction.
He created intimacy.
He created marriage.
And Proverbs does not merely tolerate marital affection—it tells the husband to rejoice in his wife.
That Hebrew word, שְׂמַח — semach, carries the idea of rejoicing, being glad, taking delight.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical faithfulness is not merely refusing everyone else.
It is learning to treasure the covenant God has entrusted to you.
And perhaps that is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because adultery usually begins long before a bedroom.
Sometimes it begins with comparison.
A husband stops noticing his wife but notices everybody else.
A wife stops speaking honestly to her husband but begins emotionally confiding in another man.
Someone feels unseen.
Someone feels lonely.
Someone enjoys being desired again.
A notification arrives.
A conversation becomes private.
Private becomes secret.
Secret becomes intimate.
And eventually the heart starts drinking from somebody else’s well.
Nobody wakes up one morning planning to destroy everything they love.
Compromise usually comes quietly.
One look.
One conversation.
One rationalization.
One deleted message.
One secret.
One more night telling yourself:
“I can control this.”
That may be why Proverbs speaks so urgently.
Because sin rarely introduces itself by announcing where it intends to take you.
It shows you the entrance.
God shows you the destination.
And sexual sin has consequences that reach far beyond a moment of pleasure.
Trust can shatter.
Children can be wounded.
Marriages can collapse.
Consciences can become numb.
Friendships can be destroyed.
Church communities can be shaken.
A person can spend years trying to rebuild what took minutes to betray.
But if you have already fallen, keep reading.
Because this is where some Christians stop the story.
Jesus does not.
Maybe you are reading this carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe you have committed adultery.
Maybe you are trapped in pornography.
Maybe your marriage is barely alive.
Maybe you crossed boundaries emotionally.
Maybe you gave your body to people who never gave you covenant.
Maybe you have been sexually sinned against and now intimacy itself feels complicated.
Maybe your history is messy enough that words like “purity” make you want to leave the room.
Please hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sexually spotless people get Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can come to Jesus and be made clean.
That does not make sin harmless.
Grace never calls darkness light.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He enters our darkness and calls us out of it.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You did this. Therefore this is who you are.”
The Gospel says:
“You sinned. Bring it into the light. Come to Christ.”
Because Jesus did not go to the cross for the imaginary version of you.
He died for sinners.
Real sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Adulterers.
The lustful.
The ashamed.
The secretive.
The wounded.
The people who promised God they would never do it again…and did.
The people who cannot believe how far they wandered.
The people who look fine in church while carrying wars nobody sees.
Christ came for people who need mercy.
At the cross, sin is not excused.
It is judged.

And the astonishing message of Christianity is that the judgment our sin deserves falls upon the willing, sinless Son of God, and those who turn to Him in faith receive forgiveness they could never purchase for themselves.
That is why grace is not permission to keep drinking from poisoned wells.
Grace gives you a reason to put the cup down.
Jesus does not merely forgive you so you can return unchanged.
He forgives.
Cleanses.
Restores.
Transforms.
Calls you to walk differently.
And sometimes repentance becomes painfully practical.
Delete the number.
End the secret conversation.
Stop protecting access to the thing destroying you.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Find mature Christian accountability.
Put boundaries around your phone.
Stop calling emotional adultery innocent because clothing never came off.
Stop feeding fantasies about somebody who does not belong to you.
If you are married, turn toward your spouse.
Talk.
Listen.
Repent where necessary.
Forgive where biblically possible.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where the wounds run deep.
Rebuild slowly.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Remember that covenant love is not maintained by emotion alone.
It is guarded by thousands of choices nobody applauds.
And if you are single, Proverbs 5 still speaks powerfully to you.
The principle is not, “Find somebody quickly so you can satisfy every desire.”
Your body does not become sovereign simply because you are unmarried.
Christian sexuality ultimately belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your desires may speak loudly.
They do not get the throne.
Jesus does.
There will be moments when obedience feels expensive.
There will be moments when temptation tells you that God is withholding something wonderful.
That lie is older than civilization.
“Did God actually say…?”
The serpent has always tried to convince human beings that God’s boundaries are evidence of God's stinginess.
But biblical boundaries are not prison bars around human flourishing.
They are guardrails around things powerful enough to destroy us when misused.
Fire belongs somewhere.
Water belongs somewhere.
Sexual desire belongs somewhere.
Proverbs calls the married person back to the covenant well.
Drink from your own cistern.
There is something almost heartbreaking about those words.
Your own.
Not somebody else’s spouse.
Not somebody on a screen.
Not the fantasy you have constructed.
Not the person sending you messages your husband or wife would be devastated to read.
Your own.
There is dignity in belonging.
There is holiness in fidelity.
There is worship in saying, when nobody would ever discover otherwise:
“No.
I belong to Christ.
And because I belong to Christ, my body does not get to make promises my soul has no right to make.”
Perhaps somebody reading this is seconds away from returning to something hidden.
This may be your interruption.
Close it.
Walk away.
Call somebody.
Pray.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
And perhaps somebody else is reading this after the damage has already happened.
Then your word is different.
Come home.
Not to pretending.
Not to image management.
Not to religious performance.
Come home to Jesus.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the screenshots.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish you could erase.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ is still Lord over what happens next.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because grace is greater.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Grace that brings sinners to their knees and then raises them into newness of life.
Grace that teaches us to say no.
Grace that rebuilds ruined people.
Grace that turns confession into freedom.
Grace that takes the sentence you thought ended your story and places a cross where you thought there could only be a period.
Maybe Proverbs 5:15 was never merely about adultery.
Maybe beneath the warning is a much larger question:
Where are you drinking?
Where are you looking for satisfaction?
Where do you run when you feel empty?
Whose attention makes you feel valuable?
What secret desire has slowly become your refuge?
Because you can be sexually faithful outwardly while your heart is dying of thirst inwardly.
And no husband or wife can ultimately carry the weight of being your savior.
Marriage is sacred.
Sexual faithfulness matters.
But even the purest marriage cannot satisfy the deepest thirst of the human soul.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
Eventually every earthly cistern reminds us that human beings were created for something greater than pleasure.
We were created for God.
Jesus said that whoever drinks the water He gives will never thirst in the same ultimate way again.
That does not erase ordinary human longing.
It tells us where longing finally has to kneel.
So guard your marriage.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your messages.
Guard your imagination.
Guard your covenant.
But above everything else, give your heart completely to Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle. But sometimes two honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.

And if God has already brought you through sexual brokenness, betrayal, addiction, shame, or a season when your marriage nearly collapsed, your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to surrender.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Let somebody reading know that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not somebody you want to shame.
Somebody you love.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget convictions we were certain about yesterday.
You may need these words again.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not compulsion, while also affirming the legitimacy of supporting those laboring to spread the Gospel.
You can still help.
Pray.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting alone with a glowing screen.
A message is waiting.
A temptation is whispering.
A marriage is hanging by a thread.
A Christian is wondering whether one secret decision really matters.
Maybe your share reaches them five minutes before a decision they cannot easily undo.
Maybe your testimony reminds them to close the door.
Maybe your comment makes another believer realize they are not the only one fighting.
Maybe Scripture reaches somebody through you.
And maybe they finally understand:
God's command was never simply,
“Do not drink.”
It was:
Do not destroy yourself drinking from a well that was never yours.
And when you discover that you already have…
there is still a Savior standing beside the ruins.
There is still repentance.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still grace.
There is still Jesus.
The well you drank from may explain your scandal—but it does not have the authority to write your ending. Jesus does.
